title: Aerodynamics
tagline: Aerodynamic forces, potential flow, airfoil theory and panel methods, finite wings, viscous drag, shocks and expansions, and transonic and supersonic flow
summary: Aerodynamics explains how wings produce lift and what it costs in drag. The course builds from aerodynamic forces and potential flow to thin-airfoil theory, panel methods, finite wings and induced drag, and viscous effects and stall, and then turns to compressible aerodynamics: oblique shocks and expansion waves, subsonic and transonic airfoils, supersonic flow and the main features of hypersonic flight.
overview: Aerodynamics is the study of how air flows around objects and the forces that result. For the mechanical engineer, aerodynamics is the foundation of aircraft design, wind turbine design, automotive design, and the design of any structure that moves through or interacts with a flowing fluid. The course begins with the fundamental forces and coefficients that describe aerodynamic behaviour, and builds through potential flow theory, thin-airfoil theory, and panel methods to the practical design tools used in industry today.

The first half of the course deals with incompressible flow: the aerodynamic forces and coefficients that define lift, drag, and pitching moment; the potential flow theory that describes the flow around bodies using superposition of elementary flows; thin-airfoil theory, which relates airfoil shape to lift and moment; and panel methods, the numerical technique that underlies modern airfoil design codes. The finite wing theory extends these two-dimensional results to three dimensions, introducing the wing-tip vortices, downwash, and induced drag that determine the performance of real wings. Viscous effects complete the picture with boundary layers, skin friction, form drag, stall, and high-lift devices.

The second half of the course deals with compressible flow: oblique shocks and expansion waves that govern supersonic flow; the Prandtl-Glauert rule, critical Mach number, and drag divergence that define the transonic regime; supercritical airfoils and sweep that delay the drag rise; and the Ackeret theory and hypersonic flow that describe flight at speeds greater than sound. The course provides the complete theoretical and practical foundation for understanding how wings work at all speeds, from the subsonic transport to the hypersonic re-entry vehicle.

The course is quantitative throughout. Every concept is expressed as a formula, every formula is illustrated with a worked example, and every example is verified by numerical calculation. The exercises progress from direct substitution to derivation, and the widget plots allow the student to explore the relationships between parameters interactively. The goal is not just to know the formulas but to develop the engineering judgement to know when and how to apply them.
outcomes: Calculate lift, drag, and pitching moment coefficients and explain their dependence on angle of attack, Reynolds number, and Mach number
Apply potential flow theory, thin-airfoil theory, and panel methods to predict the pressure distribution and forces on airfoils
Explain the origin of induced drag and calculate the lift distribution and induced drag of finite wings using lifting-line theory
Describe boundary layer development on airfoils, predict skin friction drag, and explain the mechanism of stall
Apply oblique shock and Prandtl-Meyer expansion relations to supersonic flow over wedges and airfoils
Calculate the critical Mach number and drag divergence Mach number, and explain how supercritical airfoils and sweep delay the drag rise
Apply linearised supersonic theory (Ackeret theory) to calculate lift and wave drag of thin supersonic airfoils
Describe the main features of hypersonic flow including thin shock layers, high stagnation temperatures, and real gas effects

chapters.title: Aerodynamic forces and coefficients
chapters.summary: Lift, drag and pitching moment and their coefficients, the centre of pressure and the aerodynamic centre, and the similarity parameters of aerodynamics.

chapters.title: Incompressible potential flow
chapters.summary: Stream function and velocity potential, elementary flows and their superposition, flow over a cylinder and the Kutta–Joukowski theorem.

chapters.title: Airfoils and thin-airfoil theory
chapters.summary: Airfoil geometry and nomenclature, the Kutta condition, vortex sheets, and thin-airfoil theory for lift and pitching moment.

chapters.title: Panel methods
chapters.summary: Source and vortex panel methods for airfoils of arbitrary shape.

chapters.title: Finite wings
chapters.summary: Wing-tip vortices and downwash, Prandtl's lifting-line theory, induced drag, and the effects of aspect ratio and sweep.

chapters.title: Viscous effects, drag and stall
chapters.summary: Boundary layers on airfoils, skin-friction and form drag, transition, stall and high-lift devices.

chapters.title: Oblique shocks and expansion waves
chapters.summary: Oblique shock relations, the θ–β–M relation, Prandtl–Meyer expansions and shock-expansion theory.

chapters.title: Subsonic and transonic airfoils
chapters.summary: Compressibility corrections, the critical Mach number, drag divergence and supercritical airfoils.

chapters.title: Supersonic and hypersonic flow
chapters.summary: Linearised supersonic flow over thin airfoils, wave drag, swept wings, and the main features of hypersonic flow.

history.title: Bernoulli's principle
history.detail: Daniel Bernoulli publishes Hydrodynamica, establishing the relationship between pressure and velocity that underlies all of aerodynamics.

history.title: Euler's equations
history.detail: Leonhard Euler derives the equations of motion for inviscid flow, providing the mathematical foundation for potential flow theory and the Kutta-Joukowski theorem.

history.title: Reynolds number
history.detail: Osborne Reynolds demonstrates the transition from laminar to turbulent flow, introducing the dimensionless number that governs boundary layer behaviour and skin friction drag.

history.title: Wright brothers' first flight
history.detail: Orville and Wilbur Wright achieve the first powered, controlled, sustained flight at Kitty Hawk, demonstrating that lift can be predicted and engineered.

history.title: Thin-airfoil theory
history.detail: Max Munk and others develop the vortex sheet formulation that Ludwig Prandtl and Albert Betz refine into thin-airfoil theory, relating airfoil camber to lift and moment.

history.title: Panel methods
history.detail: The source and vortex panel methods are developed for computing the flow around arbitrary airfoil shapes, the numerical technique that underlies modern airfoil design codes such as XFOIL.

history.title: Compressibility and the sound barrier
history.detail: Adolf Busemann and others recognise that the drag rise near Mach 1 is caused by local supersonic flow and shock waves, not an insurmountable 'sound barrier'.

history.title: Supercritical airfoil
history.detail: Richard Whitcomb at NASA Langley begins the research that leads to the supercritical airfoil, with its flat upper surface and aft camber to delay drag divergence.

history.title: Breaking the sound barrier
history.detail: Chuck Yeager flies the Bell X-1 past Mach 1 at Edwards Air Force Base, demonstrating that supersonic flight is achievable and opening the door to supersonic transport and military aircraft.

references.title: Fundamentals of Aerodynamics
references.note: The standard undergraduate text, covering incompressible and compressible aerodynamics with clarity and depth.

references.authors: I.C. Abbott and A.E. von Doenhoff
references.title: Theory of Wing Sections
references.note: The classic reference for airfoil geometry, aerodynamic characteristics, and section data.

references.title: Low-Reynolds-Number Airfoils
references.note: The theory and implementation of the XFOIL panel method for airfoil design and analysis.

references.title: Low-Speed Aerodynamics
references.note: A rigorous treatment of potential flow, panel methods, and lifting-line theory.

references.title: Modern Compressible Flow
references.note: The standard text for compressible flow, covering shocks, expansions, and supersonic/hypersonic aerodynamics.

references.title: A Design Overview and Status of the NASA Supercritical Airfoil
references.note: The seminal paper on supercritical airfoil design and transonic aerodynamics.

references.title: Elements of Aerodynamics
references.note: A concise and elegant treatment of classical aerodynamic theory.

references.title: Synthesis of Subsonic Airplane Design
references.note: The application of aerodynamic theory to practical aircraft design and configuration.
